content: Centaurea montana, commonly referred to as perennial cornflower, mountain cornflower, or mountain bluet, is a species of the Centaurea genus that is native to Europe. It is predominantly found in the southern mountain ranges of Europe, where it is widespread and common, but it becomes less frequent in the northern regions. This plant has a tendency to escape from cultivated gardens, which has led to its establishment in areas such as the British Isles, Scandinavia, and North America. Centaurea montana typically grows in meadows and open woodlands, particularly in the upper montane and sub-alpine zones, favoring areas with basic soil conditions. The plant reaches a height of approximately 30 to 70 cm (12 to 28 inches) and primarily flowers between May and August. It can be identified among other Centaurea species in the region by its usually entire (undivided) leaves and the distinctive blue-purple coloration of its outermost ray florets. This species can be differentiated from the cornflower (Centaurea cyanus) by its growth habit and floral characteristics. Centaurea montana is a perennial plant that typically produces a single flower head, occasionally up to three, whereas Centaurea cyanus is an annual plant with multiple flower heads. Additionally, a closely related species, Centaurea triumfettii, can be distinguished by its more narrowly-winged stems, narrower leaves, and preference for growing in rockier habitats. Although Centaurea montana is inedible, it is widely regarded as a valuable medicinal plant in Central Europe, where it has been traditionally used for various therapeutic purposes.
